own_scenes.place: Estados Unidos (Peppermint Lounge, Whisky a Go Go)
own_scenes.desc: El Twist (1960-1962) fue el gran liberador del baile social: sin pareja, libre, con poco juego de pies; tras él llegó un aluvión de bailes nacidos entre adolescentes negros y popularizados por músicos negros (el Pony, el Watusi, el Mashed Potato, el Frug, el Monkey, el Jerk), cuyo nombre iba en el título del disco. Supusieron la vuelta del cuerpo a la cultura popular blanca. Los institucionalizaron las discotecas (el Whisky a Go Go del Sunset Strip, enero de 1964, con chicas bailando en jaulas) y los programas de televisión (Shindig!, Hullabaloo, Where the Action Is). «Land of 1000 Dances», de Chris Kenner (1962), enumeraba los bailes; Cannibal & the Headhunters, del este de Los Ángeles, le añadieron el «na na-ne-na-na» en 1965. En 1966 llegó el Boo-Ga-Loo de Tom and Jerrio, mezcla de Motown, aire latino y gritos a lo James Brown, en la estela de «Let’s Dance» de Chris Montez y «Wooly Bully» de Sam the Sham, el single más vendido de 1965.

refs.q: In the modern era, it all began with the Twist
refs.para: In the modern era, it all began with the Twist – the pop sensation of 1960, 1961 and 1962 and the great liberator of social dancing. It had taken about three years for the style to pass from a small group of young black Americans to a worldwide phenomenon, and, in the early to mid-sixties, other dances rushed in to fill the frantic need for more novelty – new beats, new steps, new names – that the Twist had created through its unexpected success.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: The Twist represented nothing less than the return of the body within mainstream American popular culture.
refs.para: ‘Keep loose’, ‘really feeling it’: these were powerful instructions to the white Americans targeted by the booklet. Most of the new dances originated among teenage blacks and were popularised by black musicians. Indeed, dance records would provide their entry into the pop charts. In turn, young whites were exposed to black culture as they rarely had been before. The Twist represented nothing less than the return of the body within mainstream American popular culture.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: There was another new dance craze in 1966: the Boo-Ga-Loo.
refs.para: There was another new dance craze in 1966: the Boo-Ga-Loo. This was popularised by a comedy/singing act called Tom and Jerrio, who saw kids performing the dance at a Chicago record hop. Released in March 1965, their single ‘Boo-Ga-Loo’ welded a fast Motown rhythm to a Latin feel and James Brown-style interjections. The record went to #11 in Billboard’s R&B charts, prompting a quick follow-up, ‘(Papa Chew) Do the Boo-Ga-Loo Part 1’.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

podcast.title: Height of Popularity at Peppermint Lounge
podcast.body: The Twist dance craze was at its peak when The Ronettes, then underage, gained an accidental regular gig at the Peppermint Lounge in New York, a pivotal venue for the Twist. "They went to the peppermint lounge, just as the twist craze was at its height..."
